text.p: How could you possibly grow a business by putting your customers second?

Very successfully, according to Hal Rosenbluth, chief executive of Rosenbluth International, a Philadelphia-based travel company whose revenues grew from $20 million to more than $2.5 billion in just over a decade.
The key, he told participants at Inc. Magazine's recent annual conference of the nation's 500 fastest-growing privately held companies, is to put your employees first.
"Only when someone knows what it feels like to be first in the eyes of their employer, will they be able to do the same for the customer," he said.
Most people want to succeed at their jobs, says Rosenbluth, 45. "Nobody joins a company with a bad attitude," he said, adding that he blames companies for creating problems among their employees.

Rosenbluth says his company, which was started by his grandparents in 1892, has tried to "formalize care" among its employees. "We try to create an environment in which people care about each other. When you have a company built on friendship, everyone pulls together," he said.
"You can't fake it, the same way you can't fake farming. In business, we all try to fake things sometimes."
The company evidently doesn't fake much, as it's among the top 10 in the book The Top 100 Companies to Work for in America, by Robert Levering and Milton Moskowitz (Penguin Books).

The process begins with the job interview, where Rosenbluth combines traditional methods with an unconventional approach and interviewers aim to gauge a candidate's attitudes toward fellow employees as well as toward customers.
For senior executive positions, Rosenbluth himself gets involved.

His philosophy on developing leaders is to "find people who care an awful lot about other people and who can make a tough decision. When I find a problem," he added, "most of the time it's a leadership problem. It's tough to be a good leader."
Instead of interviewing candidates across a desk, he might take them for a drive to a Philadelphia suburb, with the candidate at the wheel.

But the candidate's replies to his questions are not what really interests Rosenbluth. He wants to see whether the candidate joins the herd in the packed left lane of the crowded expressway or instead chooses the less-crowded and much-faster right lane.

Once he invited a prospective executive to his cattle ranch in North Dakota. The man tooled around with Rosenbluth in his pickup truck, sitting in back for a couple of hours with three wailing children.
Rosenbluth later woke him in the middle of the night to go with him to check on some cows that were calving. The man passed both tests and won the job.
"Service, once you have the right people, is an emotion," Rosenbluth said. "You cannot ask someone to care 'starting next Thursday.'"

Rosenbluth says he's organised the business "like a family farm," with the various business units willing and able to help each other. Only when they are unable to solve a problem, much as a farmer may need the help of a doctor or other specialist in a nearby town, do they turn to headquarters for assistance.

It's quite a large "farm," with 4,400 employees in 1,000 locations spread across more than 40 countries. But the approach evidently works, as turnover is minimal and the company has expanded tremendously since Rosenbluth became president in 1985 and CEO in 1987.

The lesson for other business owners is simple, he says: "If you focus on the people who work for you, they will focus on the customer. It's not easy to run a company that focuses on people and friendship, but it works."

Sign on a Lodi, N.J., supplier of propane gas and grill accessories: "Sorry we missed you. If you need gas and we're closed, take one of these tanks outside the door and return it when you come to refill your tank." Talk about putting your customers first!
